title: Toboggan down from the Mutianyu Great Wall
description: Quieter than Badaling and less rugged than Jiankou, with a cable car up and a toboggan slide back down that turns the exit into the best part of the visit. Go on a weekday morning for long stretches of wall to yourself.

title: Walk the marble boat and Long Corridor at the Summer Palace
description: Empress Dowager Cixi diverted naval funds to build a stone boat that never sailed - it still sits motionless on Kunming Lake. Enter via the Beigongmen gate by subway to dodge the tour-bus crowds at the main gate.

title: Cycle the lanes around Shichahai hutong
description: Rickshaw touts here quote several times the fair rate - rent a bike instead and loop the lakes yourself. Come at dusk when the bars along the water light up and the day-trip groups have moved on.

title: Eat Peking duck carved tableside near Qianmen
description: The original Quanjude branch carves each duck into more than 80 slices at your table and serves it three ways - in a pancake, in soup, and skin dipped in sugar. Reserve days ahead or the wait can outlast the meal.

title: Eat a dumpling banquet before the Tang Dynasty show
description: Each dumpling is folded into the shape of whatever fills it, so you can tell walnut from duck before you bite. The song-and-dance show afterwards is touristy, but the orchestra plays reconstructed Tang-dynasty instruments you won't hear elsewhere.

title: Look up at the 71-metre Leshan Giant Buddha from the river
description: The stairway queue past the Buddha's ear can run two to three hours on weekends - the river boat instead shows you the whole 1,200-year-old carving from the water in twenty minutes.

title: Follow the mineral terraces up Huanglong valley
description: The turquoise and gold travertine pools sit above 3,000 metres, so altitude hits before the scenery does. Most visitors pair it with Jiuzhaigou, ninety minutes away, on the same trip.

title: Order a mandarin-duck hotpot on Jinli Ancient Street
description: Ask for a yuanyang pot split between fiery mala broth and a plain one, or the Sichuan peppercorns will numb your lips through dessert. The street is touristy, but the hotpot chains lining it are the ones locals actually queue for.

title: Stay a night in Jiaju, the watchtower village of Danba
description: A Chinese magazine once voted this the country's most beautiful village, and the stone watchtowers above the houses back it up. The roads in from Chengdu are long and winding, which is exactly why it stays quiet.

title: Wander Lijiang's canals before the day-trippers arrive
description: The cobbled lanes and canal bridges are genuinely beautiful at 7am and genuinely overwhelmed by 11. Stay the night inside the old town so you catch it quiet at both ends of the day.

title: Climb to Songzanlin, Yunnan's 'Little Potala Palace'
description: Shangri-La sits above 3,200 metres, so the stairs up to this working Tibetan Buddhist monastery hit harder than they look. Time it for the morning prayer session - the horns carry across the whole valley.

title: Cycle the shoreline loop around Erhai Lake
description: E-bike stalls line the Dali side of the lake, and the full loop runs about 120 kilometres, so most riders do a half-loop and bus back. The quieter east shore's Bai fishing villages rarely see a foreign face.

title: Trek two days into car-free Yubeng village
description: A new road reaches the outskirts, but the last stretch and the sacred waterfall beyond it are still walk-in only, under Meili Snow Mountain. Guesthouses are basic and cards don't work, so carry cash in from Deqin.

title: Cross the glass skywalk on Tianmen Mountain
description: The cable car up is one of the longest in the world, but the glass-bottomed walkway around the cliff face is where most people actually turn back. Cloth shoe covers are compulsory and do nothing to stop your legs shaking.

title: Watch lanterns light up along the Tuojiang River in Fenghuang
description: Day-trippers clear out by early evening, which is exactly when the wooden stilt houses along the river light up. Stay a night rather than passing through - the town looks like a different place after dark.

title: Cruise the Li River between Guilin and Yangshuo
description: This exact stretch of karst peaks and river is on the back of the 20-yuan note. The four-hour public cruise boat costs a fraction of the tourist ferries for the identical view.

title: Watch the light change over Longji's rice terraces
description: The terraces flood into mirrors in May and turn gold by late September - most other months they're simply green. Stay overnight in Ping'an or Dazhai village so you're already on the ridge for sunrise.

title: Bamboo raft down the quieter Yulong River
description: Every tour group in Yangshuo books the Li River - this tributary gets a fraction of the traffic for the same limestone-peak scenery, drifting past working water buffalo instead of other rafts.

title: Climb to the Potala Palace on a timed ticket
description: Tickets are capped at 2,300 a day, booked through a WeChat mini-program up to ten days out, and tied to your passport number. Arrive in Lhasa two days before your slot - the visit itself is capped at one hour and altitude hits hard on the stairs.

title: Join the kora circuit around Jokhang Temple
description: Pilgrims circle the temple clockwise along Barkhor Street, some prostrating full-length for the entire loop. Join the outer flow rather than cutting across it - going against a kora is a real offence to the people doing it.

title: Cross a 5,000-metre pass to reach Namtso Lake
description: One of the highest saltwater lakes on earth, reached by a pass higher than Everest Base Camp on the Nepal side. Altitude sickness here is a real risk rather than a theoretical one - acclimatise in Lhasa for several days first.

title: Sleep on the mountain for sunrise over Huangshan's sea of clouds
description: The famous shot - twisted pines rising from a sea of cloud - only happens for people who stayed the night on the summit. Book a mountaintop guesthouse weeks ahead; the day-trip cable car crowd never sees it.

title: Photograph the horseshoe lake at Hongcun village
description: Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon shot its rooftop scenes here, and the white-walled houses reflected in the crescent lake are why. It's an easy forty-minute add-on from Huangshan, but arrive before the tour buses for a still lake surface.

title: Get lost in Yu Garden before the bazaar opens
description: The Ming-dynasty garden opens before the surrounding bazaar, so the first hour is rockeries and koi ponds without the crowds funnelling through the shopping streets outside its walls.

title: Walk the plane-tree streets of the French Concession
description: No single sight anchors this district, which is the point - art deco villas, hidden courtyard cafes and shikumen lane houses reward walking without an itinerary. Start from Wukang Road or Anfu Road.

title: Sandboard the dunes above Crescent Lake at Dunhuang
description: A spring-fed crescent lake sits improbably among towering dunes on the edge of the Gobi. Climb for sunset rather than midday, when the sand cools enough to walk barefoot and the ridgelines throw long shadows.

title: Order yum cha at a century-old Guangzhou teahouse
description: Cantonese yum cha was practically invented in teahouses like this one, open since the 1880s. Arrive before 9am on a weekend or the trolleys of har gow and chicken feet won't reach your table for an hour.

title: Circle West Lake by bike at sunrise
description: Free to walk, ringed by causeways, and the single most photographed lake in China - so do the loop at 6am before the tour buses from Shanghai arrive. The Longjing tea plantations in the hills above make an easy add-on.

title: Trace the water pavilions of the Humble Administrator's Garden
description: The largest of Suzhou's classical gardens uses borrowed scenery - false perspective and framed views - to make half a hectare feel endless. Arrive at opening; every tour bus in Suzhou stops here by mid-morning.

title: Explore the abandoned Mughal capital of Fatehpur Sikri
description: Akbar built an entire imperial capital here and abandoned it within fifteen years, reportedly over a failed water supply. The Buland Darwaza gate is the tallest gateway in the world and still the site's showpiece entrance.

title: Take a dawn rowboat from Assi Ghat
description: Hire a rowboat here rather than at the crowded main ghat - the sun comes up directly behind the burning ghats downstream, and boatmen will cut the engine and let you drift in silence if you ask.

title: Stand inside the Kailasa Temple carved from one rock
description: Carved downward out of a single basalt hillside rather than built up block by block, it used an estimated three times the stone of the Parthenon and took over a century. See it on a separate day from Ajanta - the two sites are an hour apart and each deserves a full one.

title: Photograph the Gothic domes of Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus
description: Three million commuters still pass daily beneath these Victorian Gothic domes and gargoyles, making it one of the few UNESCO sites that's also a functioning rush-hour railway station. Shoot the facade from the traffic island across the road at golden hour - security won't let you linger inside with a tripod.

title: Cycle between the boulder-strewn ruins of Hampi
description: A single boulder-strewn square kilometre holds the ruins of what was once one of the largest cities on earth. Rent a bicycle rather than a tuk-tuk - the real reward here is stumbling on a half-buried carving with nobody else around.

title: See Mysore Palace lit by 100,000 bulbs
description: On Sunday nights and throughout the Dasara festival, close to 100,000 bulbs outline every dome and arch. Time your visit for one of those evenings or you'll only see the daytime version of the show.

title: Walk the coffee plantation trails of Coorg
description: Karnataka's hill country grows more coffee than anywhere else in India, and estate homestays let you walk the plantation trails yourself rather than book a tour. Abbey Falls is crowded by 10am - go straight after breakfast or skip it for a quieter cascade further into the estates.

title: Track daylight tigers on a Ranthambore safari
description: Ranthambore's tigers hunt by day rather than by night, making sightings far more likely here than in most reserves - but zones are allocated by lottery, so book the open gypsy jeep, not the larger canter truck, and request zones one through five for the best odds.

title: Spend a desert night on the Sam sand dunes
description: Every hotel in Jaisalmer sells the same sunset-camel-and-cultural-show package on dunes crowded with jeeps. Ask instead for a non-touristic camp further into the desert - fewer camels, no speakers, and stars all the way to the horizon.

title: Climb the City Palace terraces above Lake Pichola
description: The largest palace complex in Rajasthan took over four hundred years and twenty-two successive maharajas to build, which is why no two wings match. Climb to the upper terraces for the same lake view used in the Bond film Octopussy.

title: Ride the steam toy train through Darjeeling's tea gardens
description: The steam engine loops back on itself at Batasia to lose altitude, and the short joy ride covers only the spectacular Ghum stretch rather than the full, much slower run from the plains. Book a seat in the first carriage - the engine smoke drifts back over the rest.

title: Drift the mangrove creeks of the Sundarbans by boat
description: This is the only mangrove forest on earth where tigers swim between islands, and most visitors never see one - the boats drift the creeks for the birds, crocodiles and paw prints in the mud instead. Permits and a registered guide are compulsory; nobody goes ashore.

title: Sleep aboard a houseboat on Vembanad Lake
description: Vembanad Lake's houseboats are quieter and less nose-to-tail than the Alleppey stretch a few hours south, and the bird sanctuary here is a genuine draw in its own right, not just a backwaters add-on. Book a kettuvallam with a shaded upper deck - the midday sun on the water is brutal.

title: Spot elephants from a boat safari on Periyar Lake
description: The boat safari on Periyar Lake drifts past bathing elephants far more reliably than tigers, so set expectations accordingly. Combine it with a walk through the surrounding spice plantations, which most tour buses skip entirely.

title: Walk an elephant corridor in the Wayanad hills
description: While tour buses queue for Munnar's tea gardens, Wayanad's forests connect three states' worth of elephant corridor with barely any of the crowds. The Edakkal Caves' Stone Age petroglyphs are a two-hour scramble that most first-time visitors to Kerala never hear about.

title: See the 46-metre reclining Buddha at Wat Pho
description: The gold-leafed reclining Buddha is so large the temple was built around it rather than the other way round - you can only take in the whole 46 metres by walking its length. It's also home to the original school of traditional Thai massage, so book a session on site afterwards.

title: Get lost in Chatuchak Weekend Market
description: More than 8,000 stalls sprawl across fifteen thousand sections, and even locals carry a paper map. It only runs Saturday and Sunday - come on a weekday and you'll find the whole market shuttered.

title: Snorkel the granite bays of the Similan Islands
description: The park closes completely from mid-May to mid-October for monsoon recovery, squeezing the entire visitor season into seven months. Liveaboard dive trips reach clearer water and quieter bays than the day-tour speedboats out of Khao Lak.

title: Haggle from a boat at Damnoen Saduak floating market
description: Arrive before 8am, before the tour buses, or you'll be one paddle-boat deep in a floating traffic jam of matching sun hats. Locals now do more of their actual trading at Amphawa's weekend night market, a quieter alternative an hour away.

title: Swim the seven emerald tiers of Erawan Falls
description: Each of the seven tiers has its own swimming pool, and the water gets more turquoise the higher you climb - the seventh tier requires a genuine hike and thins the crowds out fast. Tiny fish will nibble the dead skin off your feet if you sit still too long.

title: Ride the Death Railway across the Bridge on the River Kwai
description: The steel bridge is a reconstruction - Allied bombing destroyed the original - but the train still crosses it several times a day and you can walk the track between services. The nearby museums make clear how many Allied POWs and forced labourers died building the line, a detail the postcards skip.

title: Walk the cutting at Hellfire Pass memorial
description: POWs and conscripted labourers hand-carved this rock cutting at night by torchlight, which is how it got its name. An audio guide narrated by survivors plays as you walk the original trackbed, and the walk down is far easier than the humid climb back up.

title: Spot wild elephants in Khao Yai National Park
description: One of Thailand's oldest national parks and a UNESCO site, with wild elephants, gibbons and hornbills within three hours of Bangkok. Book a ranger's night safari truck - that's when the elephants actually come out onto the roads.

title: Swim into Maya Bay on Koh Phi Phi Leh
description: The Beach put this bay on the backpacker map and nearly loved it to death - it now closes for a few hours a day and caps boat numbers to let the coral recover. Take the first or last boat of the day to beat the crowd, not the closure window.

title: Dance on the sand at a Koh Phangan Full Moon Party
description: It runs monthly regardless of season, so check the actual full moon date before booking - it isn't always a weekend. Buckets of spirits are sold everywhere on Haad Rin beach and are stronger than they taste; the ones in glass bottles are safer bets than the plastic ones.

title: Get your open-water diving certificate on Koh Tao
description: More divers are certified on this small island than almost anywhere else on earth, which has pushed course prices lower than most of Southeast Asia. Whale sharks turn up most reliably between March and May, though nobody can promise you one.

title: Photograph the electric-blue Wat Rong Suea Ten
description: Built decades after its more famous white neighbour, this working temple uses a deep cobalt blue you won't find on another temple in Thailand. It's small enough to see properly in under an hour, so pair it with the White Temple the same morning.

title: Stand where Thailand, Laos and Myanmar meet at the Golden Triangle
description: The Mekong and Ruak rivers meet exactly at the point where three countries touch, and a viewpoint and small opium museum explain how this stretch once supplied much of the world's heroin. Riverboat trips out for a closer look at the Laos side are cheap and easy to arrange riverside.

title: Watch sunset from the ridgelines of Pai Canyon
description: The sandstone ridges narrow to barely a metre wide in places with a genuine drop on both sides, and there's no fencing at all. Come an hour before sunset and keep walking past the first viewpoint - most visitors stop there and the crowd thins out fast beyond it.

title: Stroll Hua Hin's night market after a royal seaside stay
description: Thailand's oldest beach resort, still anchored by a royal summer palace, and calmer than Pattaya or Phuket because it grew up around Thai holidaymakers rather than international package tours. The night market seafood grills are some of the best value in the country.

title: Dodge the macaques at Lopburi's monkey temple
description: Several thousand long-tailed macaques run the ruins of Phra Prang Sam Yot and have learned to unzip bags, so carry nothing you can't afford to have stolen and eaten. Every November the town throws them an actual buffet, piling fruit pyramids in front of the temple for the Monkey Buffet Festival.

title: Eat your way down Chiang Mai's Sunday Walking Street
description: The old city's main road closes to traffic every Sunday evening and fills with food stalls, hill-tribe crafts and temple courtyards turned into massage stops. Go hungry and graze rather than sit down anywhere - the khao soi and grilled skewers are better spread across several stalls than committed to one.

title: Cruise overnight through Ha Long Bay's limestone islands
description: Overnight on a junk boat rather than day-tripping - the bay only really reveals itself once the tour boats clear out and you're alone with 1,600 limestone islands at sunset. If the crowds put you off, neighbouring Bai Tu Long Bay gets a fraction of the boat traffic for the same scenery.

title: Trek the world's largest cave at Son Doong
description: The world's largest cave passage is big enough to fly a 747 through, has its own weather system, and a jungle growing inside a collapsed section of ceiling. Only one operator holds the permit, tours run a few hundred people a year, and it books out roughly a year in advance.

title: Wander the Nguyen emperors' citadel in Hue
description: The Nguyen emperors modelled their citadel on Beijing's Forbidden City, right down to a Forbidden Purple City at its heart - much of which was shelled to rubble during the 1968 Tet Offensive and is still being rebuilt piece by piece. Go early to see the outer walls before the tour groups and the heat both arrive.

title: Row the coconut canals of Ben Tre
description: Ben Tre grows more coconuts than anywhere else in the country, and a combination of rowboat, bicycle and horse cart gets you into canals too narrow for the bigger Mekong tour boats. Watch the coconut candy get pulled and cut by hand before you buy a bag - it's fresher than anything sold upriver.

title: Walk the boardwalk into Paradise Cave
description: At 31 kilometres this is one of the longest caves in Asia, though the public boardwalk only covers the first kilometre - still enough cathedral-scale chambers to make Son Doong feel like a rumour rather than a must. It's a far easier add-on if the multi-day expedition caves are out of budget or time.

title: Dive the reefs off Nha Trang
description: Vietnam's most developed beach city has traded some charm for high-rises, but the diving and snorkelling around the offshore islands is still the best accessible stretch of coast in the country. The mud baths at Thap Ba are touristy but genuinely soothing after a dive day.

title: Ride the world's longest cable car to Phu Quoc's Hon Thom
description: The world's longest over-sea cable car connects the mainland to Hon Thom island in under fifteen minutes, but the better reward is Sao Beach's sand, which stays soft and cool even at midday. Visit a fish sauce factory while you're here - Phu Quoc's is considered the country's best and nothing like the smell suggests.

title: Race a jeep up Mui Ne's white sand dunes
description: Jeep drivers race up the white dunes at dawn specifically so you beat both the heat and the tour buses - by 9am the sand is too hot to sit on and the light has gone flat. The red dunes nearby are smaller and quieter, without the sledding-for-tips hustle of the white ones.

title: Climb 500 steps to the Hang Mua viewpoint
description: Five hundred uneven steps lead to a dragon statue perched above the exact view used on half of Vietnam's tourism posters - a river bending through karst peaks and rice paddies below. Go for sunrise or late afternoon; the steps have zero shade and the stone turns furnace-hot by midday.

title: Spin through Cam Thanh's coconut basket boats
description: This coconut forest was a Viet Cong hideout during the war and is now where every visitor gets spun in dizzying circles inside a round bamboo basket boat by boatmen who treat it as a competitive sport. An Bang beach nearby is the quieter alternative to Hoi An's main strip.

title: Cross the Golden Bridge at Ba Na Hills
description: Two giant stone hands appear to hold up this golden footbridge 1,400 metres above sea level, a design so photogenic it went viral within weeks of opening. The cable car up holds a Guinness record for length, but arrive at opening or you'll queue longer for the bridge than you spend admiring it.

title: Watch the noon ceremony at the Cao Dai Great Temple
description: Cao Dai blends Buddhism, Christianity, Taoism and Confucianism under one giant Divine Eye, and the noon ceremony is open to respectful visitors watching from the upper balcony. Most people see it as a rushed stop bolted onto a Cu Chi Tunnels day trip - it deserves the morning slot instead.

title: Confront the war at the War Remnants Museum
description: The Agent Orange exhibits are graphic and deliberately unfiltered, and it's not a museum every visitor is ready for on their first day in the country. The captured tanks and aircraft in the courtyard outside are the easier, more digestible half of the visit.

title: Boat through Tonle Sap's floating villages
description: Southeast Asia's largest freshwater lake swells to five times its dry-season size each monsoon, and entire villages of houseboats and stilted homes rise and fall with it. Go with a small operator rather than a mass tour boat - some larger tours have been criticised for treating the community as a photo backdrop rather than a place people live.

title: Walk the Killing Fields at Choeung Ek
description: An audio guide narrated by survivors leads you past mass graves where bone fragments and cloth still surface after heavy rain. Pair it with Tuol Sleng prison in the morning - doing both back to back is heavy, but doing only one leaves half the story untold.

title: Explore the overgrown corridors of Preah Khan
description: Built as a Buddhist university for over a thousand monks, its corridors are longer and its crowds thinner than Ta Prohm's, despite the same tree-root drama. The central sanctuary's narrow, dark passageway was deliberately built disorienting.

title: See the emerald Buddha at Phnom Penh's Silver Pagoda
description: The floor is laid with more than five thousand silver tiles, most now covered by carpet to protect them from foot traffic. Shoulders and knees must be covered to enter, and the Royal Palace next door closes for a long lunch break - check opening times before you plan around it.

title: Swim the bioluminescent water off Koh Rong
description: Plankton in the shallows light up electric blue when disturbed after dark, best seen on a moonless night away from the beach bars' lights. The island has no roads at all, so onward travel between beaches is by boat or jungle footpath.

title: Ride Battambang's bamboo train
description: A bamboo platform on two axles powered by a small motor reaches surprising speed on the old rail line, and when two trains meet, whichever has fewer passengers gets dismantled and lifted off the track. It's a leftover workaround from a barely functioning railway, now kept running mostly for visitors.

title: Eat Kampot-pepper crab at Kep's crab market
description: Fishermen sell straight off their boats to the row of shacks behind the market, who cook it to order with green Kampot peppercorns still on the stalk. Order it fried with the pepper rather than steamed - it's the version every stall here is actually known for.

title: Stand on the clifftop at Preah Vihear temple
description: Perched on a cliff edge on the Thai border with views for miles across the plains below, this pre-Angkorian temple sees a fraction of Angkor's visitors because of how remote it is. Border tensions have closed it before, so check current access before making the long drive out.

title: Give alms to the monks at dawn in Luang Prabang
description: Hundreds of monks file silently past before sunrise to collect rice from kneeling townspeople, a six-hundred-year-old daily ritual now watched by more tourists than participants some mornings. Buy your rice from a local vendor rather than a tour-group stall, and keep a respectful distance rather than shoving a camera at head height.

title: Count thousands of Buddha statues in the Pak Ou Caves
description: Pilgrims have been leaving small Buddha images in these Mekong river caves for centuries, and nobody has ever counted the total. Take the slow boat upriver rather than the speedboat - the two-hour cruise past riverside villages is as much the point as the caves themselves.

title: Hike the karst viewpoints above Nong Khiaw
description: A fraction of Luang Prabang's tourists make it this far up the Nam Ou river, despite karst scenery that rivals Vang Vieng's. The steep, unmarked climb to the Pha Daeng viewpoint takes about ninety minutes and has no railings at the top.

title: Chase waterfalls across the Bolaven Plateau
description: A motorbike loop links a string of waterfalls and coffee farms across Laos's main coffee-growing plateau, cool enough at altitude to need a jacket in the morning. Tad Fane's twin drop is the highlight, but Tad Yuang draws a fraction of the crowd and sits close enough to swim underneath.

title: Climb the pre-Angkorian temple ruins of Wat Phou
description: Older than Angkor and built along the same mountain-temple cosmology, the ruined stairway climbs to a sanctuary with a natural spring the Khmer once believed sacred. Come at opening to have the mountainside mostly to yourself before the heat and the day-trippers from Pakse arrive.

title: See the gold stupa of Pha That Luang
description: This gold-covered stupa appears on the national emblem and the currency, and most Lao people consider it the country's holiest site. The surrounding cloister of smaller stupas is almost always empty even when the main stupa draws a crowd.

title: Boat through the pitch-black tunnel of Kong Lor Cave
description: A longtail boat carries you 7.5 kilometres through a limestone mountain in total darkness except for a single headlamp, the river sometimes barely deeper than the boat's hull. It floods and closes without warning in the wet season, so confirm it's running before you detour out here.

title: Watch sunset from the covered stairway up Mandalay Hill
description: A covered, mostly shaded stairway of over a thousand steps climbs past shrines to a 360-degree platform over the old royal city grid below. Go barefoot like everyone else - shoes are left at the bottom - and start ninety minutes before sunset to reach the top with light to spare.

title: Cross the world's longest teak footbridge at sunset
description: Built from recycled teak salvaged from a royal palace, the 1.2-kilometre bridge fills with monks and cyclists silhouetted against the lake at sunset - a view now crowded with photographers who know it too. Walk to the far end, away from the viewpoint crowds, for a quieter angle.

title: Watch men gold-leaf the Mahamuni Buddha at dawn
description: Devotees have pressed so much gold leaf onto this ancient bronze image that its surface is now several centimetres thick and lumpy in places. Only men are permitted to approach and apply gold directly to the statue; women watch from the surrounding hall.

title: Float over 2,000 temples in a Bagan sunrise balloon
description: Balloons only fly in the dry season and only with calm dawn winds, so operators cancel more mornings than tourists expect and rarely offer refunds for weather. Book the earliest slot available - the temple plain is at its stillest and mist still clings to the ground before the tour buses arrive.

title: Paddle the floating gardens of Inle Lake
description: Tomatoes grow on floating beds of woven water hyacinth anchored to the lake bed, tended from canoes rather than on foot, and supply much of the country's tomato harvest. Combine it with the Ywama market, which rotates location on a five-day cycle rather than running daily.

title: Trek two days from Kalaw to Inle Lake
description: The route crosses Pa-O and Danu hill-tribe farmland and ends with a boat across Inle Lake to Nyaungshwe, rather than backtracking by road. Guesthouses en route are basic and unheated, and November mornings at altitude are colder than most visitors pack for.

title: Ride the loop of Yangon's Circular Train
description: The three-hour loop circles the city's outskirts, and vendors board at each stop selling betel nut, quail eggs and whatever produce came in that morning. There's no schedule worth memorising - just show up at a station and take whichever direction leaves first.
